title: The Black Belt: Name, Geography and Change

grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Multiple strong sources or a primary source directly establishing the claim; contradictions absent or resolved.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Credible institutional or scholarly source(s); plausible, but single-sourced or secondary.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Plausible inference or weakly sourced claim; needs primary confirmation.
grade_definitions.UNRESOLVED: Sought, not found; no usable evidence in this pass.

claims.claim: The Southern 'Black Belt' was originally named for dark, fertile soil (a crescent across Alabama and Mississippi over decomposed limestone), before the term acquired demographic and racial associations.
claims.source: Encyclopedia.com (Columbia Encyclopedia), 'Black Belt' entry; Reconsidering the Southern Black Belt (ResearchGate, peer-reviewed article)
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com: the crescent was 'named for the region's unusual dark, fertile soil, underlain by deposits of decomposed limestone'; the article traces later demographic meaning. ResearchGate article agrees the term's primary original referent was soil/geology.
claims.notes: Foundational definition. Sibling work corroborates.

claims.claim: The term's meaning shifted in the 19th century from soil to the cotton-plantation labor regime and then to Black-majority counties — a racial geography layered on a soil name.
claims.source: Encyclopedia.com 'Black Belt'; MDPI Land (2026) study of Black Belt counties
claims.evidence: Both sources describe the sequence: soil region -> plantation slavery -> predominantly Black population -> racial regional label. MDPI: 'the plantation agriculture of the antebellum era, dependent upon enslaved African labor, gave the region its demographic signature.'
claims.notes: The semantic sequence is the load-bearing finding for the whole brief.

claims.claim: W. E. B. Du Bois titled a chapter of The Souls of Black Folk (1903) 'Of the Black Belt' and wrote 'This is the Black Belt of Georgia' (Dougherty County), codifying the term as a racial-geography label beyond Alabama.
claims.source: The Souls of Black Folk, full text (americanliterature.com); Wikipedia chapter summary (corroboration)
claims.evidence: Chapter VII text: Du Bois describes 'the Black Belt of Georgia' and Dougherty County as its west end. Exact quotation verified in the primary text.
claims.notes: Demonstrates the term was a recognized racial label by 1903, pre-dating Chicago usage.

claims.claim: The Southern term reached Chicago plausibly via Black migrants' own vocabulary during the Great Migration (1916-1930), though white journalists or Chicago School sociologists applying a familiar Southern term are equally plausible vectors. No direct documentary evidence of the transfer was found.
claims.source: Weak general website asserting migrants 'took the term' north, citing Richard Wright (NOT cited as evidence); Encyclopedia.com pairing of Southern/Chicago usages
claims.evidence: Semantic sequence is demonstrable (C-01..C-03, C-06); chronology fits the migration; but no dated letter, speech, or newspaper record names the transfer moment or agent.
claims.contradictions: No source directly contradicts; none directly confirms.
claims.notes: Largest uncertainty of the brief. Explicitly excluded from VERIFIED claims. Research next: migrant letters, Defender correspondence, Urban League case files.

claims.claim: Pre-1900 Black Chicago concentrated on the Near South Side: 1880s, 16th-24th Streets west of State; by 1890, the major district ran 24th-35th Streets between Federal and State Streets.
claims.source: City of Chicago, Chicago Black Renaissance Literary Movement landmark report (PDF)
claims.evidence: Report text states the 1880s settlement band and the 1890 24th-35th / Federal-State district explicitly.
claims.notes: Institutional synthesis, not contemporary primary testimony. Do not retroject 'Black Belt' as a contemporary 1890s label.

claims.claim: By September 1922 the term was established Chicago vernacular: the Chicago Commission on Race Relations' The Negro in Chicago used the scare-quoted 'so-called 'Black Belt,'' implying the name predated the report rather than originating in it.
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, The Negro in Chicago (University of Chicago Press, Sept 1922), via Project Gutenberg transcription
claims.evidence: Report text: 'the so-called 'Black Belt'' (District I of the riot geography). Scare quotes + 'so-called' mark established vernacular.
claims.notes: Strongest single documentary anchor of the brief. Public domain; maps are visual candidates.

claims.claim: The commission's retrospective 'Black Belt in 1910' covered 12th-55th Streets, Wentworth-Indiana, where Black residents were only about 10% of the population — showing coarse units exaggerate the belt's extent.
claims.source: Logan et al., 'Emergent Ghettos: Black Neighborhoods in New York and Chicago, 1880-1940' (PMC, peer-reviewed), citing CCRR 1922 p.106
claims.evidence: Article states the 1910 aggregation and the ~10% figure, and discusses enumeration-unit effects on perceived concentration.
claims.notes: Methodological anchor for §15: boundaries are functions of units and purposes.

claims.claim: The 1919 riot geography defined District I 'Black Belt' as 22nd-39th Streets (Wentworth Avenue to the lake) and 39th-55th Streets (Clark Street to Michigan Avenue), with 39th-55th (Michigan Avenue to the lake) labeled a 'contested area.'
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, The Negro in Chicago (1922)
claims.evidence: Report's riot-district definitions, transcribed at Gutenberg. Corroborated by Chicago Magazine 2019 summary (22nd-39th, Wentworth-State).
claims.contradictions: None on the definitions; note these are analytic/administrative polygons, not the colloquial belt.
claims.notes: Date-stamped polygon; not to be presented as the single definitive boundary.

claims.claim: A 1917 Chicago Tribune survey placed the Black district between 22nd and 63rd (Cottage Grove to State) and quoted Rev. L. K. Williams (Olivet) estimating 125,000 Black residents 'in quarters formerly provided for 50,000.'
claims.source: Chicago Tribune, 1917 (via Chicago Race Riot 1919 Commemoration Project excerpt); Rev. L. K. Williams quotation
claims.evidence: Commemoration Project quotes the Tribune survey and the Williams overcrowding figure.
claims.notes: The excerpt found does not use the term 'Black Belt' — evidence the place was newsworthy before the name is documented in print here.

claims.claim: Black press used the term by 1922: Dr. A. Wilberforce Williams's Chicago Defender column described Michael Reese Hospital as in the center of Chicago's 'Black Belt.'
claims.source: UIC Mapping Care project page reproducing/citing the 1922 Defender column
claims.source_type: institutional digital project citing historical newspaper
claims.evidence: Project page attributes the 'Black Belt' description of Michael Reese Hospital's location to Williams's 1922 Defender column.
claims.notes: Second-hand citation of the primary column; the column itself was not viewed. Grade accordingly. No verified 1910s Defender use found.

claims.claim: The 1922 commission reported about 90% of Chicago's Black residents lived in the designated Black Belt; its densest-zone count (Roosevelt Rd-39th, Wentworth-lake) found 54,906 Black and 42,797 white residents — a concentration, not a monoculture.
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, The Negro in Chicago (1922)
claims.evidence: Report text gives the ~90% figure and the Roosevelt-39th/Wentworth-lake population counts.
claims.notes: The 90%-of-people vs composition distinction is load-bearing.

claims.claim: University of Chicago sociologists (Park, Burgess) adopted 'Black Belt' as an academic label for Chicago's South Side Black territory in the 1920s.
claims.source: ResearchGate article on Chicago School sociology (secondary)
claims.evidence: Article states Park and Burgess labeled the territory 'Black Belt.' Consistent with the Chicago School's ecological vocabulary.
claims.notes: Single secondary source; the 1922 commission predates the textbook usage, so scholars did not coin the Chicago term.

claims.claim: Drake and Cayton (Black Metropolis, 1945) distinguished the imposed 'Black Belt'/'Black Ghetto' from the 'Black Metropolis' — 'The Black Belt became the Black Metropolis in the twenty years between the close of the First World War and the beginning of the Second' (p.77); 'Stand in the center of the Black Belt — at Chicago's 47th St. and South Parkway.'
claims.source: St. Clair Drake & Horace Cayton, Black Metropolis (1945), via Everand full-text excerpt; Harvard dissertation quoting p.77
claims.evidence: Both quotations verified in the text excerpts. The Belt/Ghetto vs Metropolis distinction is the book's analytic core.
claims.notes: Establishes the non-synonymy finding of §16.

claims.claim: Working boundaries: 1920s belt ran State (west) to Cottage Grove (east), 31st (north) to 47th (south); 1940s belt ran Cermak (north) to South Chicago Avenue (south), LaSalle (west) to Lake Michigan (east).
claims.source: Chicago Urban League, CULtivate Part 1 report (PDF), synthesizing census data; UIC 1940 census map
claims.evidence: Report text gives both polygons; the 1940 map corroborates the 1940s extent.
claims.contradictions: None; these are synthesis polygons, not contemporary self-descriptions.
claims.notes: Re-grounded from sibling material via the CUL report directly.

claims.claim: Major media used 'Black Belt,' 'Black Ghetto,' and sometimes a slur for the district, and many Black residents resented those labels.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago, 'Bronzeville' entry (Christopher Robert Reed)
claims.evidence: Entry text states the media labels and resident resentment explicitly.
claims.notes: Motivates the Bronzeville counternaming (§09).

claims.claim: 'Bronzeville' was coined in 1930 by James J. Gentry, theater editor of Anthony Overton's Chicago Bee; the Bee sponsored a 'Mayor of Bronzeville' contest in 1930; Gentry moved to the Defender in 1932 where the promotion flourished.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago, 'Bronzeville' entry; corroborated by uchicago.edu 'Voices' press history and moderncities.com
claims.evidence: EoC entry gives Gentry, 1930, the Bee contest, and the 1932 Defender move. Two independent corroborations.
claims.notes: Establishes Bronzeville as a deliberate Black-press counternaming campaign.

claims.claim: The Chicago Race Riot of 1919 Commemoration Project dates the district's renaming to 'Bronzeville' to 'the 1930s.'
claims.source: Chicago Race Riot 1919 Commemoration Project
claims.evidence: Project text: migrants settled in 'a narrow strip that came to be known as the 'Black Belt''; 'In the 1930s, this neighborhood came to be called Bronzeville.'
claims.notes: Independent institutional corroboration of the 1930s renaming.

claims.claim: Exact first use of 'Bronzeville' is disputed: the institutionally documented account gives 1930 (Gentry); sibling research surfaced an unverified 1922 account.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago (1930) vs. sibling CTL research note (1922, unverified)
claims.source_type: institutional encyclopedia vs. internal research note
claims.evidence: 1930 account fully documented (C-16); 1922 account not re-verified in this pass.
claims.contradictions: The two dates are in direct conflict.
claims.notes: 1930 is best-supported; 1922 remains possible pending a dated primary newspaper instance.

claims.claim: FSA photographs (Russell Lee, Edwin Rosskam, April 1941) document the belt's built fabric; the Library of Congress's African-American Mosaic exhibition captioned a Lee photo 'Apartment Building in Chicago's 'Black Belt'' and glossed the district's internal class geography (poorest north, elite south).
claims.source: Library of Congress Prints & Photographs Division item records (FSA-OWI, 'No known restrictions'); LOC African-American Mosaic exhibition mirror (igmlnet.uohyd.ac.in)
claims.evidence: LOC item records for Lee/Rosskam Chicago photos; exhibition page text with the 'Black Belt' caption and north-poor/south-elite gloss.
claims.notes: The 1941 photos are cleared visuals (V1-V3). The north/south class gloss is the exhibition's, single-sourced.

claims.claim: The Encyclopedia of Chicago dates common use of 'Black Belt' for Chicago 'from the turn of the 20th century until after World War II.'
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago, 'Black Belt' entry
claims.evidence: Entry text states the usage period; bibliography cites CCRR 1922, Drake & Cayton, Philpott.
claims.contradictions: Memory/scholarly use persists after WWII (C-22, C-23) — the claim is about common living use.
claims.notes: Supports the postwar-fade analysis (§10).

claims.claim: By mid-20th century about three-quarters of Chicago's Black population lived in the belt's broad footprint — a roughly 30-block strip along State Street rarely more than seven blocks wide.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Black Belt (Chicago)' citing Encyclopedia of Chicago; sibling CTL-DR-BCI-001
claims.evidence: Corroborated across two independent citational lines, but thinly sourced in both.
claims.notes: Kept at SUPPORTED per the sibling red-team warning about single-sourced superlatives.

claims.claim: Resident memory preserves the term after its living use faded: historian Timuel Black recalled growing up in the 'Black Belt' as growing up 'in a city within a city.'
claims.source: University of Chicago official YouTube channel, 'Growing up in Chicago's 'Black Belt' - Timuel Black' (video viewed; description verified)
claims.evidence: Video title, description, and credits (Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection) verified by viewing the page. Black (AM'54) is a documented Chicago historian.
claims.notes: Illustrates the inside-meaning of the term; used as video V-A, never as sole evidence for a boundary claim.

claims.claim: The NPS Black Metropolis thematic nomination (1985) uses 'Black Belt' in quotes as the historic name for the South Side Black community's 'long narrow strip' — bounded by railroad/industrial properties west, affluent white neighborhoods east, extending from Van Buren Street to 39th Street.
claims.source: National Park Service, Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (received 1985-11-07)
claims.evidence: Nomination text quoted verbatim via NPS NPGallery.
claims.notes: Shows the term's persistence as a historical label in official preservation prose.

claims.claim: c.1925 the Second and Third Wards — described as 22nd-51st Streets, Cottage Grove (east) to the Rock Island Railroad (west) — were the Black Belt/Black Ghetto core later renamed Bronzeville.
claims.source: Encyclopedia of Chicago, 'Bronzeville' entry
claims.evidence: Entry text gives the ward bounds and the label sequence.
claims.notes: A political (ward) boundary, not a vernacular one — keep the distinction.

claims.claim: Chicago Magazine (2019) summarized the 1919 Black Belt as running 'from 22nd Street (now Cermak Road) south to 39th Street (now Pershing Road) and from Wentworth Avenue east to State Street.'
claims.source: Chicago Magazine, 2019 (centennial coverage)
claims.evidence: Article text; consistent with CCRR District I's northern half (C-08).
claims.contradictions: Slightly narrower (to State, not the lake) than the commission's riot polygon — consistent with colloquial vs administrative difference.
claims.notes: Corroborates C-08's northern segment.

claims.claim: Sibling-derived: pre-1915 settlement corridors, interwar expansion, and housing-restriction mechanisms (covenants, violence, redlining, public housing, urban renewal) as the forces constraining/reshaping Black settlement.
claims.source: CTL-DR-BCI-001 / CTL-DR-BVM-005 (sibling packages)
claims.evidence: Sibling claim ledgers; partially re-grounded here via C-05, C-14, C-19.
claims.notes: Used as context only; this brief's original argument does not rest on sibling authority alone.

claims.claim: Sibling-derived population scale: Black Chicago 44,103 (1910); ~110,000 (1920); 1,102,620 (1970).
claims.source: CTL-DR-BCI-001 (sibling, graded VERIFIED)
claims.evidence: Sibling ledger; cited for scale only.
claims.notes: Not independently re-verified in this pass.

claims.claim: Earliest dated Chicago newspaper use of 'Black Belt' in the 1910s — sought in this pass (1922 commission, UIC Mapping Care Defender material, 1917 Tribune excerpt) and not found.
claims.source: Negative search across sources above
claims.evidence: No 1910s dated instance located; earliest secure print use is 1922 (C-06, C-10).
claims.notes: Research next: Defender/Bee/Tribune/Daily News sweep 1915-1925.

claims.claim: Whether federal housing agencies' (HOLC/FHA) own documents used 'Black Belt' for Chicago was not checked in this pass; the brief makes no claim about it.
claims.source: Out of scope for this pass
claims.evidence: None gathered.
claims.notes: Do not assert agency usage.
